clue.text: Taken for a ride by gangster, triumph then fly

parts.note: a hood, short for hoodlum, is a gangster
to triumph is to win
a ked is a wingless parasitic fly found on sheep

explanation.surface: A mobster's victory followed by his getaway, someone's tale of being driven off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken for a ride' reads as gangland abduction but here means deceived. KED is an obscure word for the sheep ked, a bloodsucking fly.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken for a ride is an idiom for being tricked or duped, which is exactly what being hoodwinked means.

clue.text: Result of getting 19 in German city around midnight?

indicators.note: the city's name wraps itself about the single letter from the centre of night

parts.note: Hanover is a city in Lower Saxony, Germany
the middle letter of the word night

explanation.surface: Asks what follows a late night out in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is BLADDERED (very drunk), so the result is the morning-after condition. 'midnight' is read literally as the middle of 'night'.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting very drunk is followed the next day by a headache and nausea, the classic consequence of excessive drinking.

clue.text: See 1
Day and date during good month for a bit of Mendelssohn?

parts.note: Wed is the short form of Wednesday
in can mean during, as in 'in the night'
March is a month of the year

explanation.surface: Planning a wedding day in a pleasant month, with suitable music in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' looks like a containment signal but simply gives IN as part of the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Mendelssohn's incidental music for A Midsummer Night's Dream includes the famous processional played as brides leave the church.

clue.text: Women seen through curtains? They're not the sober type

indicators.note: the letter for women appears through, that is within, the curtains

parts.note: nets are net curtains

explanation.surface: Women glimpsed behind net curtains, apparently tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the British saying 'as pissed as a newt', meaning very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially these amphibians are the drunkest of creatures, so humorously they are never sober.

clue.text: Stupid as one Conservative MP, with ale leading to Labour candidate's complaint

indicators.note: stupid suggests the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one is I
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dim Tory MP and beer combine to give a Labour Party candidate a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour candidate' is not a politician but a woman about to give birth.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a dangerous condition of pregnancy involving seizures, so it afflicts an expectant mother approaching childbirth.

clue.text: Ring male that's caught in the firing line

parts.note: a ring is shaped like the letter O
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
he is a male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man caught inside a ring, in the line of fire.
explanation.walkthrough: In darts the oche is the line players stand behind when throwing, so 'firing line' is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: The throwing mark in darts is where the player launches their darts, a playful version of a firing line.

clue.text: Fruit of ruby red colour, half gone off

indicators.note: off as in gone bad suggests the letters spoil into another order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the first half of the word colour survives, the rest being gone

explanation.surface: A deep red fruit whose colour has partly faded as it goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half gone' leaves COL from 'colour', and 'off' then shuffles RUBYRED with COL.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an orange-amber berry of northern moorland, related to the bramble, so it is an example of a fruit.

clue.text: Larks with all but topless chicks?

indicators.note: topless means losing the first letter of the word

parts.note: all but means almost or nearly
chicks and birds are both slang for young women

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of skylarks with nearly naked young women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' takes the N off NEARLY. Larks here are people, not birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A lark is a person who rises early in the morning, the opposite of a night owl.

clue.text: Good-for-nothing Born to Run live disc is included

parts.note: née means born, used before a maiden name
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: the disc is included within the word for live

parts.note: to dwell is to live somewhere
a disc is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A wastrel who plays Springsteen's Born to Run live, disc and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born to Run' looks like the Springsteen song title but splits into NEE and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are terms for a worthless, idle person who never amounts to anything; they are synonyms.

clue.text: 24/6? Starting from zero initially, usual reckoning …

indicators.note: starting picks out the first letter of the word from

parts.note: zero looks like the letter O

indicators.note: initially takes the first letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: Reads as a calculation done from scratch by ordinary arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: '24/6' looks like a date, 24 June, but here it is a division sum; the next clue uses the date sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Twenty-four divided by six gives this number, so the sum defines it.

clue.text: What a sidekick plays, using spare racket

parts.note: a second, as in a second car, is a spare one
a racket and a fiddle are both swindles

explanation.surface: A sidekick playing tennis with a borrowed spare racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' suggests tennis but means a scam.
explanation.definitionFit: To play this part is an idiom for taking a subordinate role, as a sidekick does to the hero.

clue.text: … involves one adding 24/6

indicators.note: the noon word wraps around, so involves, the one who adds

parts.note: the ellipsis points to this clue's own number, twelve, which as a time is noon
a summer is one who sums, that is adds up

explanation.surface: Continues the sum of the previous clue: someone adds up to get the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis sends you to the clue's own number, twelve, read as a time of day. Here 24/6 is a date, 24 June, not the division of the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenty-fourth of June is the traditional English quarter day marking the height of the season.

clue.text: Kiss on the lips? Puck will, getting into trouble for minor misconduct

indicators.note: on the lips means as spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a peck is a quick kiss

indicators.note: the setter's 'I will' gets into the word for trouble

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble
Puck is the setter, so he will is I'll

explanation.surface: The setter planning a sneaky kiss and landing himself in hot water.
explanation.walkthrough: PECC is only a sound-alike of PECK. 'Puck will' becomes I'LL because Puck is the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sin or trivial fault is called by this Spanish-derived word, so it means a minor offence.

clue.text: Cooking apple, large and sour, useful in many ways

indicators.note: cooking suggests the letters are prepared into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sour cooking apple, a big one, handy for many recipes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking apple' reads as a Bramley but 'Cooking' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something versatile, suitable for several uses, is described by this adjective; they are synonyms.

clue.text: People praising one of those late goals use it excitedly, without beginning to apologise

definitions.text: People praising one of those late

indicators.note: excitedly suggests the letters are jumbled about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the beginning of the word apologise is its first letter

explanation.surface: A footballer celebrating a last-minute goal wildly without saying sorry.
explanation.walkthrough: Shuffle GOALS USE IT, 'without' the A from 'apologise'. 'one of those late' is the deceased, not a late goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who give speeches of praise at a funeral honour someone who has died, the late person.

clue.text: Sandwich and a little drink as well? Not quite in amounts produced in a summer's day

definitions.text: amounts produced in a summer's day

parts.note: a sub is a submarine sandwich
a tot is a small measure of spirits

indicators.note: not quite means the word falls short of its last letter

parts.note: also means as well

explanation.surface: Ordering a sandwich and a little drink too, then totting it up.
explanation.walkthrough: A summer is one who adds, so a summer's day is spent totting up figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Partial sums are worked out along the way by someone adding up, a punning use of summer.

clue.text: Partaking of booze killed wrestling champion

indicators.note: partaking of means taking a share of the words, so the letters sit inside them

explanation.surface: Drink did for a wrestling champion.
explanation.definitionFit: In sumo this is the second-highest rank, just below grand champion yokozuna.

clue.text: Setter almost flipped — health resort has no Special Brew

indicators.note: flipped means the shortened name is turned backwards
almost means the setter's name loses its last letter

parts.note: the setter of this puzzle is Puck

indicators.note: has no means the letter for special is removed from the resort

parts.note: a spa is a health resort

explanation.surface: The setter flips out because the spa has no Special Brew lager.
explanation.walkthrough: Special Brew is a strong British lager, which makes 'Brew' look like beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A brew is British slang for a mug of tea, which is also called by this informal word.

clue.text: Born to Run in tights? Journalist is very drunk

parts.note: a run in tights is a ladder, a line of broken stitches
ED is the usual short form of editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist turns up very drunk, with laddered tights, to Born to Run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born to Run' again splits up: B, then 'Run in tights' as LADDERED. BLADDERED is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang word means extremely intoxicated, a colloquial synonym for being very drunk.

clue.text: Executive position, brewing cider — sort drunk with joint

indicators.note: brewing means the letters of cider are fermented into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters of sort stagger into another order

parts.note: taken as written
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Brewing cider and getting drunk, with a joint too, hardly executive behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewing' turns CIDER into DIREC and 'drunk' turns SORT into TORS.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat on a company board is an executive post, the office held by a director.

clue.text: Film buff

definitions.meaning: the 1996 Australian film about pianist David Helfgott
to buff is to polish until it gleams

explanation.definitionFit: The title of a 1996 film, and also a verb meaning to polish.

clue.text: Lacking support, like the Yard after a third cut

definitions.meaning: having no foundation or leg to stand on

definitions.text: like the Yard after a third cut
definitions.meaning: a yard of three feet with a third removed is short by one ...

explanation.surface: Scotland Yard's budget slashed by a third, leaving it unsupported.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital Y suggests Scotland Yard, the London police, but it is the measure of three feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without feet has nothing to stand on, so it has no support; a third off a yard leaves it one foot short.

clue.text: See 22
Play instrument, backing …

indicators.note: backing means the word for instrument runs backwards

parts.note: a tool is an instrument

explanation.surface: Instructs someone to play an instrument as backing music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' is the noun: Joe Orton's 1965 black comedy. The ellipsis leads to the next clue, about words that read the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of Joe Orton's farce, so it is an example of a stage play.

clue.text: … Abba or A-ha? Do-re-mi plan scuppered

indicators.note: scuppered means wrecked, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Two pop bands' do-re-mi singing plans fall apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Abba and A-ha look like the bands but are cited as words reading the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Both band names spell the same forwards and backwards, so each is an example of such a word.

clue.text: Newspaper article covering page in dictionary

indicators.note: the dictionary covers, that is surrounds, the letter for page

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about a page in a dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion piece printed opposite the editorial page is a type of newspaper article.

clue.text: Females once carrying a torch for Puck perhaps, rejected after enjoyment outside front of house

indicators.note: after places the reversed setter after the enjoyment part
the word for enjoyment sits outside the house letter

parts.note: use can mean enjoyment, as in the legal term for having the benefit of something

indicators.note: the front of the word house is its first letter
rejected means the setter word is sent back the other way

parts.note: Puck is an example of a crossword setter

explanation.surface: Women who once carried a torch for the setter, but rejected him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying a torch' suggests unrequited love; cinema attendants literally carried torches (flashlights). 'front of house' is also theatre jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinema attendants, mostly women, once showed patrons to their seats using a flashlight.
